featured_reviews.name: Gopal Pandia
featured_reviews.review_text:
Standing proudly beside the Arabian Sea, the Gateway of India is one of the most iconic landmarks in Mumbai and a place that truly captures the spirit of the city. The grand architecture, inspired by Indo-Saracenic style, looks even more beautiful in real life than in pictures. The detailed design, huge arch, and historical importance make this place a must-visit for every traveller.

The atmosphere around the monument is always lively. You can see tourists taking photos, local people enjoying the sea breeze, street vendors selling snacks, and ferries moving across the water towards Elephanta Caves. Early morning and evening are the best times to visit because the weather feels pleasant and the view during sunset is absolutely stunning.

One of the best parts about visiting here is the location itself. Right beside the Gateway stands the famous Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, which adds even more charm to the area. The entire surroundings feel energetic and full of history. Security arrangements are good, and the area is mostly clean despite being crowded.

The place can get very busy during weekends and holidays, so visiting on a weekday is a better option if you want to enjoy peacefully. Parking nearby can be difficult, and local taxi or cab services are usually more convenient. There are many food stalls and cafés around where visitors can enjoy Mumbai’s famous snacks after exploring the monument.

Overall, the Gateway of India is not just a tourist spot, it is an experience that reflects the culture, history, and beauty of Mumbai. A perfect place for photography, sightseeing, and spending quality time with family or friends. Definitely worth visiting at least once.

featured_reviews.name: Shubham Prince
featured_reviews.review_text:
I visited Gateway of India mainly to head to Elephanta Caves and honestly, this is where you need to be careful.
Many ticket sellers will confidently tell you the ticket is for Elephanta Caves, but in reality, some of them are just round-trip joy rides that bring you back to the Gateway itself.
Important note:
If you’re actually going to Elephanta Caves, make sure:
1. You go before 3 PM
2. The ticket price is around ₹130 or more Cheaper tickets are usually not for the caves — learned this the hard way.
The place is extremely crowded, the heat can be brutal, and you’ll need patience. The vibe is energetic though, street noise, tourists everywhere, boats lining up, and the iconic view of the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel right in front of you.
Plenty of photographers will approach you. If you do get photos clicked, ask for digital copies. The printed versions are honestly poor in quality and not worth it.
Overall experience?
The enthusiasm is there, the atmosphere is lively, but it does feel a bit overhyped. Not bad, not amazing  just… fine.
Still, it’s one of those places you experience once, observe everything, question a few things internally, and move on.
Enjoy your time at the Gateway — just go informed.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Rajabai Tower, University of Mumbai: The Mumbai University is undoubtedly one of the finest examples of Victorian Neo Gothic
Architecture in Mumbai. It is also an integral part of one of the finest urban ensembles of Victorian buildings in the world. The Rajabai Tower, with its imposing skyline, dominates the skyline of the Fort area, thus further strengthening its classification for reasons of scenic value.
The Mumbai University, designed by Sir Gilbert Scott, is an example of a public project in the city funded by local philanthropists, in this case, the "Cotton King" of Bombay, Premchund Roychund who made a generous contribution of Rupees 4 lakhs towards its construction. As a gesture of acknowledgment, the lofty Rajabai Tower, an awesome structure that rose to a height of 260 feet, was named after his mother. The Library structure adjoining the Rajabai Tower has among the finest ensembles of stained glass in the country while the splendid cross vaulted roof of the Reading Room with its polished timber members, is among the most spectacular architectural interiors in the city.

featured_reviews.name: Rahul
featured_reviews.review_text:
Beautiful place which is seen from city
The 142-year-old Rajabai Clock Tower in South Mumbai’s Fort area, located inside University of Mumbai’s campus, is iconic for its Victorian-Gothic architecture. Built in 1878 by architect Sir George Gilbert Scott, it was commissioned by businessman Premchand Roychand as a tribute to his mother, hence the name. For years, it was the city’s tallest structure, at 285 feet. Rajabai Clock Tower has long been a beacon of the Oval Maidan precinct, a visual delight, and a valuable piece of history for the city. After brilliant restoration work by SNK Consultants, the clock tower was handed over to KSA Lighting Designers in 2017 for lighting the tower, the facade and the interiors of the University Library. Kanchan Puri, principal at the firm, tells us the process of this massive undertaking that was completed recently. After years of darkness, the Rajabai Clock Tower finally glowed up in 2021, literally.

featured_reviews.name: Х. У. З.
featured_reviews.review_text: I called to book my tour the same morning and was happy that they were able to accommodate me last minute! Aamir was my guide for the slum and laundry tour - he clearly knew where he was going and what he was doing, and although I could tell he had walked the same route many times before, it didn’t feel touristy or artificial at all. It just felt like we were walking through a neighborhood he knew well, where more or less everything was open to the outside world. We started off in the area where there are many small factories for clothing, recycling, and bakery products - at every little business we encountered, he simply had to ask to enter, and we could walk right in and see the process up close. It was fascinating to me - I never would have imagined that the bread I buy in a supermarket or clothes I buy in a normal store come from such small-scale operations and not major, industrial manufacturing plants. We also passed through a residential area, and I even stopped to get henna done from a woman we met at random while inside her neighbor’s pottery studio. For that reason, we didn’t have a lot of time towards the end, and the laundry was just a stopover at the lookout over the area (where I was mobbed by vendors trying to sell me things; an expected part of being an outsider in India), but overall it felt like a very authentic look into the everyday lives of much of Mumbai’s lower class. I took a private tour so I wasn’t in a big group, and I’m not that much into taking photos so we moved very fast - which is what I preferred as there was so much to see. Highly recommended.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Mumbai Port Trust (also known as the Bombay Port Trust) is a port which lies midway on the West coast of India, on the natural deep-water harbour of Mumbai (Bombay) in Maharashtra.The harbour spread over 400 square kilometres (150 sq mi) is protected by the mainland of Konkan to its east and north and by the island city of Mumbai to its west. The harbour opens to the south to the Arabian Sea.The port is administered by the Mumbai Port Trust (MbPT, formerly the Bombay Port Trust (BPT)), an autonomous corporation wholly owned by the Government of India.The port is primarily used for bulk cargo, while most container traffic is directed to Nhava Sheva port across the harbour.Mumbai Harbour has been used by ships and boats for centuries. It was used by the Maratha Navy, as well as the British and Portuguese colonial navies. In 1652, the Surat Council of the East India Company, realising the geographical advantage of the Port, urged its purchase from the Portuguese. Their wish was gratified nine years later when, under the Marriage Treaty between Charles II of Great Britain and the Infant Catherine of Portugal, the ‘Port and Island of Bombay’ were transferred to the king of Great Britain The first of the present-day docks of the Port were built in the 1870s.Bombay Port Trust (BPT) was established as a corporation on 26 June 1873.BPT's founding chairman was Colonel J.A. Ballard.

Port development was undertaken by the civil engineering partnership Sir John Wolfe-Barry and Lt Col Arthur John Barry as Joint Consulting Engineers to the Bombay Port Trust at the end of the nineteenth century.

From its establishment, the port has been the gateway to India, and was a primary factor in the emergence of Mumbai as the commercial capital of India. The port and the corporation took their present names in the 1990s.

Over the decades, the port underwent tremendous expansion, with the addition of berths and cargo handling capacities. However, Mumbai's expanding growth and population pressure constrained the growth of the port by the 1970s. This led to the establishment of the Nhava Sheva port across Mumbai Harbour in Navi Mumbai on the Konkan mainland. Nhava Sheva began operations in 1989, and most container traffic now flows through Nhava Sheva. With a minimum draft of 6.9 metres (23 ft). Victoria Dock, commissioned in 1891, had 14 berths as of 2008 with a minimum draft of 6.7 metres (22 ft). Indira Dock, commissioned in 1914, had 21 berths, with a minimum draft of 7.0 metres (23.0 ft). Prince's Dock and Victoria Dock are semi-tidal docks, with vessels docking and departing at high tide. Indira Dock has a lock, enabling vessels to enter or depart at any time. The port has four jetties on Jawahar Dweep, an island in the harbour, for handling Crude and petroleum products. These jetties have a draft of 12.2 metres (40 ft). Liquid chemicals are handled from a jetty on Pirpau.

Ballard Pier Extension has a passenger terminal, including immigration clearance facilities for crews and passengers of cruise liners.

The port has a total of 69 anchorage points. A pilot is mandatory for all vessels of over 100 tonnes net weightage.

featured_reviews.name: Amy
featured_reviews.review_text:
Review of South Mumbai

South Mumbai, often called the heart of the city, is where history, luxury, and urban life blend seamlessly. From colonial-era architecture to upscale shopping streets and breathtaking sea views, this part of the city offers a unique charm that sets it apart.

Architecture & Heritage

One of South Mumbai’s biggest draws is its stunning architecture. Landmarks like the Gateway of India, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT), Bombay High Court, and the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel reflect the city’s rich colonial past. The area is a paradise for history lovers, with well-preserved Victorian-era buildings giving it a distinct old-world charm.

Culture & Lifestyle

South Mumbai is home to art galleries, theaters, museums, and cultural hubs. Places like Kala Ghoda, Jehangir Art Gallery, and the National Gallery of Modern Art attract art enthusiasts, while Marine Drive and Girgaum Chowpatty offer a peaceful retreat by the Arabian Sea. The nightlife here is vibrant, with high-end bars, clubs, and fine-dining restaurants.

Shopping & Dining

From the luxury boutiques of Colaba and Palladium Mall to the street shopping at Fashion Street and Crawford Market, South Mumbai caters to all kinds of shoppers. The dining scene is equally diverse, offering everything from iconic Irani cafés like Kyani & Co. to fine-dining establishments like The Table and Wasabi by Morimoto.

Transport & Accessibility

South Mumbai is well-connected by local trains, buses, and taxis, but traffic congestion can be a major issue, especially during peak hours. The Mumbai Metro expansion is expected to improve connectivity in the future.

Overall Experience

South Mumbai is where Mumbai’s heritage, culture, and modern luxury come together. Whether you’re a history buff, a foodie, a shopaholic, or just someone who enjoys a scenic sunset by the sea, this part of the city has something for everyone.

Rating: 4.8/5
A must-visit area that captures the true essence of Mumbai, though traffic and high costs can be a drawback!

The Heart of Mumbai's Cricket and Heritage!

"Oval Maidan is a vast and vital green space in the Fort area, providing a much-needed open area in the busy South Mumbai.

It is most famous for its role in Mumbai's cricket scene, with countless matches being played simultaneously, especially on weekends.

It is a fantastic place to witness the city's passion for the sport.

The Maidan is bordered by stunning Victorian Gothic and Art Deco architecture, including the Bombay High Court and the University of Mumbai, which makes for a beautiful and historic backdrop.

It serves as an excellent spot for a morning run, an evening stroll, or just relaxing under the shade of a tree.

While it can get busy, the Oval Maidan is essential to the city's spirit and a perfect place to experience local life and admire Mumbai's rich architectural heritage."

featured_reviews.name: Sakib Mulla
featured_reviews.review_text:
Occupying a majestic 22-acre expanse in the heart of South Mumbai,the Oval Maidan is a sublime palimpsest of colonial grandeur and contemporary leisure. Enveloped by the architectural duality of the Victorian Gothic revival to the east and the sleek Art Deco ensembles to the west now collectively enshrined as a UNESCO World Heritage site the ground serves as a verdant bridge between centuries.
To traverse its periphery is to witness a sophisticated choreography of Mumbai’s social fabric. Under the watchful shadow of the Rajabai Clock Tower, the air is thick with the rhythmic thwack of willow against leather, as aspiring cricketers populate the dusty pitches in a relentless pursuit of sporting excellence. The maidan functions as a civic lung, exhaling a serene tranquility that contrasts sharply with the frantic kinesis of nearby Churchgate.
The aesthetic appeal lies in its unmanicured authenticity; it is neither a rigid botanical garden nor a chaotic wasteland, but a curated void that permits the city to breathe. As the golden hour bathes the limestone gargoyles of the High Court in amber hues, the Maidan transcends its physical boundaries, becoming a temporal sanctuary. It is an indispensable urban theater where history remains a living, breathing participant in the everyday life of the metropolis. For the discerning visitor, it offers a peerless vantage point to observe the architectural and cultural heartbeat of Mumbai.

🚉 Must-visit experience in Mumbai — seriously, don’t miss this!

If you think you know Mumbai, think again. The “Crown Jewel of Mumbai” Heritage Tour at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) is an absolute show-stopper. For just ₹500 on BookMyShow (and yes, no walk-ins — exclusivity adds to the thrill 😉), this guided tour unlocks parts of CSMT most Mumbaikars have only rushed past while chasing trains.

The journey takes you through the Heritage Gallery, Railway Museum, Central Dome, and the stunning Star Chamber — and trust me, this is one train you’ll want to slow down for. You’ll uncover jaw-dropping British-era history, architectural secrets hidden in plain sight, and UNESCO heritage spaces that finally make you stop, stare, and look up (literally and emotionally).

We often travel or visit distant places to see historic architecture, but having something this magnificent right in Mumbai is really special. These details usually go unnoticed, but once you start observing, the beauty becomes very evident.

featured_reviews.name: TheR Side
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visiting Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is not just about seeing a railway station — it feels like witnessing a living piece of Indian history. This iconic landmark of Mumbai is one of the most beautiful railway stations in the world and a proud symbol of India’s architectural heritage. Built in 1887 during the British era to celebrate Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, the station was originally known as Victoria Terminus (VT). Later, it was renamed in honor of the great Maratha king Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.

The architecture of CSMT is truly breathtaking. Designed by British architect Frederick William Stevens, the building is a perfect blend of Victorian Gothic Revival style and traditional Indian architecture. Every corner of the station showcases detailed stone carvings, massive domes, pointed arches, stained glass windows, wooden ceilings, iron structures, and artistic statues. The central dome with the statue holding a torch represents progress and development. Even after more than a century, the structure still looks grand and royal.

What makes this place truly special is that it is not just a railway station — it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Mumbai’s greatest identities. Millions of people travel through this station every day, making it one of the busiest railway stations in India. Yet beyond the crowd and trains, CSMT stands as a symbol of Mumbai’s spirit, history, culture, and nonstop energy. The station has appeared in many Bollywood movies, documentaries, and photographs because of its iconic beauty and historic importance.

The construction itself was considered an engineering masterpiece of its time. Huge stones were brought from different places, and skilled Indian craftsmen worked for years on the carvings and decorations. The building combines advanced British engineering with Indian artistic craftsmanship, which is why it still stands strong today. At night, when the entire structure lights up, it looks absolutely magical and royal.

Whether you love history, photography, architecture, or travel, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is a place everyone should experience at least once. It is not just a station where trains arrive and depart — it is the heartbeat of Mumbai, a masterpiece of art and engineering, and a timeless monument that tells the story of India’s colonial past and modern progress together.

featured_reviews.review_text:
CST is one of the most iconic and historically rich railway stations in India. The architecture is absolutely stunning, with intricate detailing and a grand design that reflects a perfect blend of Victorian Gothic style and Indian craftsmanship. It’s not just a station—it feels like a heritage monument.
The station is well-connected and always full of energy, showcasing the true spirit of Mumbai. Watching the constant movement of people and trains adds to its unique charm.
However, like most busy stations, it can get very crowded, especially during peak hours, which may feel overwhelming for some visitors.
Overall, a must-visit place for its historical significance and architectural beauty.

featured_reviews.name: Vijender Singh
featured_reviews.review_text:
CSMT is one of the best connected railway stations in Mumbai and a perfect base if you want to explore the city. The station itself is a UNESCO World Heritage Site – beautiful old architecture, huge space and a constant buzzing vibe.

What makes CSMT amazing is how close it is to most major tourist spots in South Mumbai. Within 10–20 minutes you can reach places like Gateway of India, Marine Drive, Colaba Causeway, Crawford Market, Girgaon Chowpatty, Haji Ali, Worli Sea Face and many more. Taxis, buses and even metro connectivity are easily available right outside the station.

It also connects very smoothly to other major stations like Byculla, Dadar, Kurla, Wadala Road, Sewri, Sandhurst Road and gives quick access to both Central and Harbour lines. Plenty of food options, ATMs, luggage areas and local shops are available inside and around the station.

If you’re visiting Mumbai or planning a quick day trip around South Mumbai, starting from CSMT makes everything super convenient. Safe, historic, well-connected and surrounded by most of the city’s iconic locations.

featured_reviews.name: Joby Jacob
featured_reviews.review_text:
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) is much more than just a busy train station -it is the ultimate symbol of Mumbai. It is a protected world heritage site, and the building itself is stunning. It looks like a grand, old European castle mixed with an Indian palace, complete with beautiful stone carvings, a massive dome, and colorful stained-glass windows.
Step inside, and you will see the real magic of Mumbai. During rush hour, the station fills up with thousands of locals rushing to work. It is crowded, loud, and fast-paced, but watching this organized chaos is an incredible experience. If you love taking photos, the building looks spectacular at night when all the colorful lights are turned on.

featured_reviews.name: Piyush Tomar
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visited Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) in 2026 and observed the station mainly from the outside. The building continues to be one of Mumbai’s most iconic landmarks, with its stunning Victorian Gothic architecture standing out beautifully, especially during the evening when it is well-lit. The structure is well-maintained and gives a grand, historic vibe that reflects the city’s heritage.

However, the surrounding area outside the station is quite busy and chaotic, which is expected given its central location. There is constant movement of taxis, buses, and local commuters, making the area crowded throughout the day. While the roads are functional, traffic management could still be improved to reduce congestion and make pedestrian movement smoother.

Cleanliness outside the station is decent but not consistent. Certain areas are maintained well, while some corners still need better upkeep and regular cleaning. The presence of street vendors adds to the local experience, but at times it contributes to crowding and slight clutter around entry points.

Security presence is visible, and there are barricades and checkpoints that help manage the flow of people. Lighting at night is a big plus, making the area feel relatively safe and visually appealing.

Overall, the outside view of CSMT is a mix of heritage beauty and typical Mumbai hustle. It’s a must-visit spot for its architecture and vibe, but improvements in cleanliness and crowd management would make the experience much better.

featured_reviews.review_text: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is not just a railway station, it’s a living heritage monument. featured_reviews.name: Swapnil Chaudhari (swap)
featured_reviews.review_text:
Flora Fountain in Mumbai is a stunning heritage monument that beautifully blends Neo-Gothic and Indo-Sarcenic architecture. Sculpted from imported Portland stone, it features a graceful 7-ft statue of the Roman goddess Flora atop, surrounded by four corner figures symbolizing the seasons.

Built in 1864 at a then sizeable cost of ₹47,000, it marks the intersection of five busy roads in Fort, historically dubbed the "Piccadilly Circus of Mumbai."  Over time, the square was renamed Hutatma Chowk to honor martyrs of the Samyukta Maharashtra movement.

After years of disrepair, the fountain underwent a major restoration. Engineers rediscovered its original water plumbing system — there are 64 spouts, including lion-head and fish-shaped ones — and restored water flow to full glory.  During renovation, a concealed chamber with antique valves and even old bottles was found, lending to its historical mystique.

Today, it's not just a monument but a lively urban hub, surrounded by book stalls and heritage walks. Though traffic swirls around, the illuminated fountain at night offers a quiet, poetic escape.

Verdict: A must-visit for heritage lovers, photographers and anyone wanting a peaceful moment in the bustle of South Mumbai — it’s a timeless gem steeped in history.
